narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Stolen Dance That Won the Cake
This is Cakewalk. Mid-19th century to early 20th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (LqpINmqxlsc)
Title card: Cakewalk · United States · Mid-19th century to early 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Developed from mid-19th-century prize walks on Southern US plantations, the cakewalk was exhibited at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.
It moved into minstrel shows and eventually Broadway, starring performers like Dora Dean and Charles E. Johnson, before becoming an international sensation in Paris in 1903.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed during Sunday gatherings and nighttime parties as a recreational pastime and a covert satire of white aristocratic European dances, with slaveholders awarding cakes to winning couples.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Utah -- The Desert Paradise.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/Utah_--_The_Desert_Paradise.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: A lively partnered vernacular jazz dance featuring processional walking, high-stepping kicks, struts, slides, and an erect upper body tilted backward, alternating with frantic jumps and turns.
Watch for The High-Stepping Strut, The Chalkline Walk.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (LqpINmqxlsc)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: couples in a processional circle or line, moving down a central space
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Notated in a 2/4 time signature with an oompah rhythm, incorporating syncopation, polyrhythms, and habanera rhythms.
Historically played with banjos and violins, it heavily shaped the development of ragtime.
Listen for the banjo, violin.
The pulse is 2/4.
A lively 2/4 march with a heavy oompah beat, enriched by syncopated ragtime rhythms, banjos, and violins.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wore handed-down finery including top hats, swallow-tail coats, large bow ties, canes, and long ruffled hoop skirts.
Settings ranged from plantation yards to rented halls with banked spectator tiers.
on_screen: Image gallery: 8 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dora Dean, Charles E. Johnson, Tom Fletcher, Eugénie Fougère, Aida Overton Walker, Will Marion Cook.
Spread from Florida across Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and New York, reaching international popularity in Paris and influencing early tango styles in Buenos Aires.
Rooted in African American plantation culture, influenced by the ring shout, and serving as a direct precursor and sibling style to ragtime music.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Cakewalk is influence of Ragtime: Many early ragtime tunes were actually cakewalks, sharing identical musical antecedents.
Cakewalk is shares music of Tango: The arrival of the cakewalk and ragtime in Buenos Aires in 1903 influenced early styles of tango.
Cakewalk is variant of Lindy Hop: Early 1900s cakewalk steps are preserved and performed within the modern Lindy Hop community.
